reasoning: The previous guidance emphasized applying the exact theorem and carrying its conclusion through, but nine failures persisted, so that advice was not specific enough to change the choice process. The errors show failures in both directions: the agent underclaimed established results (full residual freeness, an if-and-only-if classification, strict log-concavity, and a global valuative-independence statement) while also accepting unsupported additions (such as an extra expansion or an insufficiently justified threshold). The recurring issue is not simply choosing a claim that is too weak or too strong; it is failing to verify the precise distinction between plausible options. There were no regressions, and the one improvement—choosing the precise O(√n log n) estimate rather than the exponent shorthand—suggests that careful comparison of quantitative formulations can help. Ten stable successes indicate no broad loss of the skill. The updated guidance makes the option contrast itself the target of verification, while retaining the need to support every clause.
slow_update_content: For a specialized theorem-based question, use the answer choices to identify the exact disputed clause before deciding; do not answer from topic recognition or from an instinct to choose either the safest or the strongest-sounding option. For each plausible choice, isolate what it adds, omits, or changes relative to the shared claim, then actively verify that difference from the applicable result or a derivation. Check both whether a fuller conclusion is established and whether any added refinement, exception, scope, rate, or coefficient is unsupported; do not automatically downgrade a complete result or promote an attractive embellishment. When the distinction is a classification, verify both directions; when it is quantitative, compare the actual thresholds and hypotheses. Choose the fullest claim whose every clause is established, and do not substitute a remembered neighboring result for an unverified exact statement.
update_target: Address longitudinal regressions and persistent failures observed across adjacent epochs.
